newsitem.title: RUSSIA: LUKoil wise to eye expansion - analysts.
newsitem.headline: LUKoil wise to eye expansion - analysts.

text.p: Russia's biggest oil firm LUKoil, eager to insulate itself from the economic and political risks of producing crude in Russia, is wise to eye foreign projects, energy analysts said on Wednesday.
"It needs to get away from Russia to get away from the political risk," said Stephen O'Sullivan, associate director of oil and gas at MC Securities in London.

LUKoil President Vagit Alekperov said on Tuesday that the company was close to a final deal to buy a five percent stake from U.S. major Chevron Corp in the Tengiz oilfield in Kazakhstan, one of the world's newest energy frontiers.
Alekperov also said LUKoil hoped to sign an agreement next month to resurrect a stalled, billion-dollar project to develop Iraq's Western Kurna oil field.
"I think this move does make sense, because the problem LUKoil faces is the fact that it is 99 percent a Russian oil company," O'Sullivan said, referring to the Tengiz plan.
The two projects bring LUKoil closer to its dream of becoming the first Russian star on the international oil stage.
"The Tengiz deal fits very well with LUKoil's whole strategy of becoming an international company," said James Bunch, energy analyst at brokerage Renaissance Capital.

LUKoil already has a 12.5 percent stake in Azerbaijan's flagship $8 billion Azerbaijan International Operating Company (AIOC) consortium of 13 international companies that will begin tapping Caspian reserves in August.
Analysts said that by eyeing assets abroad, LUKoil reduces the financial risks of developing intensively its 7.9 billion barrels in reserves in remote Western Siberia.
"LUKoil has made no secret of its strategy to move 25 percent of its production out of Russia by 2000," said Peter Houlder, managing director of the CentreInvest consultancy.
"The opportunities in their own (Siberian) regions are becoming increasingly constrained, both geologically and geophysically."
One analyst said LUKoil could even seek ways into upstream and downstream projects in the North Sea, South America, Angola and Vietnam, as well as in Eastern Europe.
LUKoil already has a deal with the Atlantic Richfield Co (ARCO) of the United States to spend at least $3 billion on joint Russian and overseas projects.
LUKoil's strategy -- which many observors say was masterminded by consultancy McKinsey and Co -- has political as well as economic dimensions.
"LUKoil has the support of the Russian government," O'Sullivan said. "In a way, LUKoil is acting as a representative for state policy."
Kazakhstan is eager to have LUKoil's involvement because Russia still controls most of the pipeline system in Central Asia used to transport crude to Western markets.

Russia's rising star oil company, already a darling with foreign investors, will in Tengiz work side-by-side with Chevron, which now has a 50 percent stake, and Mobil Corp of the United States, which has a 25 percent stake.

LUKoil produced around 58.0 million tonnes of oil in 1996, or 1.16 million barrels per day, about one-sixth of Russia's total output, with 1997 output forecast to edge up to 60.0 million tonnes (1.20 million bpd).
